newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcy debt soars, outlook bleak.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcy debt soars, outlook bleak.

text.p: The scale of Japanese corporate bankruptcies rose sharply last month and the outlook is bleak as the economy struggles to achieve solid recovery, a private research company said on Friday.

The firm, which specialises in bankruptcy data, said total debts held by companies which folded in November leapt 49.6 percent from a year earlier to 1.55 trillion yen ($13.7 billion) after a wave of big corporate failures. The figures were the worst in 14 months.
The latest in a string of bad bankruptcy data, the liability figures from Tokyo Commerce and Industry Research Co highlight the lingering frailty of the economy.
The report also said there would be no early respite from the high level of business failures, citing signs that the economy may slip back into a slump after a planned sales tax hike next year.

"Consumption activities are becoming increasingly restrained in light of the expected increases in the sales tax and utility charges as well as uncertainty in the outlook for incomes," Tokyo Commerce said.
The failures in November included major realtor Sueno Kosan, which collapsed with debts of about 716 billion yen ($6.33 billion). It was the second-largest insolvency in Japan since World War Two.
Sueno borrowed heavily from failed "jusen" mortgage firms. Total debts of Sueno and its two group firms were 975 billion yen ($8.62 billion), the report said.

Large-scale bankruptcies involving debts of more than one billion yen ($8.8 million) surged to 75 in November from October's 48. In October, bankruptcy debt nearly doubled from a year earlier to 1.36 trillion yen ($12 billion), although the number of cases fell slightly year-on-year.
The number of companies filing for bankruptcy rose 6.8 percent from a year earlier to 1,339.
The reasons cited were weak economic conditions, sluggish sales, accumulated losses and problems collecting money owed.
"The number of corporate failures, especially among small- and medium-sized companies, continues to be at a high level amid changes in the industrial structure," Tokyo Commerce said.
It expects failures to total around 14,950 in 1996, down only slightly from the 15,108 last year and up from 14,061 in 1994.
"Although some industries such as personal computers, mobile phones, automobiles and housing are doing well, the trickle-down effect on other industries is limited," it said.

The prop of government spending on public works, which has helped bolster the economy up to now, is also due to disappear as the projects run their course, while private sector capital outlays are expected to remain generally sluggish.
In November, the number of bankruptcies in the service sector was up 18.3 percent from a year earlier at 161, and those in the construction sector rose 12.6 percent to 365.
Bankruptcies in the real estate sector fell 28.1 percent from a year earlier to 46 cases.
